b: Search volume is the number of times people type a given query into a search engine over a defined period, almost always expressed as an average per month. It exists because advertisers and publishers need a way to size demand before they spend money or write a page: a keyword searched 50,000 times a month can support a campaign or an article that a phrase searched 20 times cannot. The figure is never a raw count supplied in real time. Every public number, from Google's Keyword Planner to third-party SEO databases, is an estimate that has been averaged, rounded, grouped or modelled before it reaches the user.

The reference source for most of the industry is Keyword Planner, the research tool inside Google Ads. Its headline metric, "Avg. monthly searches", is defined by Google as "the average number of times people have searched for a keyword and its close variants." By default, according to the Google Ads Help Center, "the number of searches for the term (regardless of language) is averaged over a 12-month period." Changing the location, the date range or the network settings changes the result.
Several processing steps sit between the search box and the figure on screen:

Averaging. A 12-month mean flattens seasonality. A term searched 200,000 times in December and 5,000 times in July can show an annual average near 21,000, a number that matches neither month. Keyword Planner offers monthly breakdowns for that reason.

Close-variant grouping. Plurals, misspellings and some abbreviations are pooled. Google states that historical statistics such as average monthly searches "are only shown for exact matches," and that the match type chosen for a campaign does not change them.
Rounding. Google says "your search volume statistics are rounded," which is why volumes for individual cities rarely add up to the national total.

Ranges for low-spend accounts. Since 2016, accounts without meaningful active spend see buckets rather than numbers: 0, 1-100, 100-1K, 1K-10K, 10K-100K, 100K-1M and 1M+, according to Search Engine Land.

Keyword Planner sits next to related metrics that are often read together with volume. Competition (low, medium or high) measures "the number of advertisers that showed on each keyword relative to all keywords across Google." Top-of-page bid estimates give a low range, an approximation of the 20th percentile of bids, and a high range near the 80th percentile, based on the last 30 days.

Microsoft offers its own figures. The Microsoft Advertising Ad Insight API operation GetHistoricalSearchCount "gets the number of times the normalized term was used in a search during the specified time period," aggregated by device type. Data can be pulled daily for up to 45 days back, weekly for up to 15 weeks, or monthly for up to 24 months, with up to 1,000 keywords per request. Amazon exposes search demand through Brand Analytics as a search frequency rank rather than an absolute count, so marketplace volume is a ranking, not a number.

SEO platforms such as Semrush, Ahrefs, Moz and SISTRIX publish volumes for billions of phrases, far beyond what any one Keyword Planner account can extract. Their numbers are modelled. The usual inputs are Google's own data (often ranged), clickstream panels that record browsing behaviour from opted-in devices, and rank-tracking data that maps queries to results pages. Each vendor weights these differently, which is why the same phrase can show 1,900 searches in one tool and 4,400 in another.

Clickstream supply has proved fragile. Jumpshot, an Avast subsidiary that claimed a panel of more than 107 million consumers and 150 billion clicks a month, was shut down in January 2020 after reports about its data sales. Avast chief executive Ondrej Vlcek said the operations would be "immediately terminated," according to Search Engine Land. Several research tools relied on that data, the same report noted, without naming them.

The scale of the long tail explains why modelled data matters. Keywords with fewer than 10 searches a month make up almost 93% of Ahrefs' US database of roughly 2.3 billion phrases, while just under 18,000 keywords exceed 100,000 monthly searches, figures collected in PPC Land's explainer on long-tail queries. Google has repeated since 2013 that about 15% of daily queries have never been seen before, which means no historical volume exists for them at all.

Google Trends is frequently confused with a volume tool. It publishes no absolute figures. As PPC Land's Google Trends explainer sets out, each data point is divided by total searches for that geography and period, then scaled from 0 to 100, where 100 marks the peak for the chosen settings. Two terms with very different absolute volumes can both read 100. Low-volume terms return zero, repeat searches are stripped, and Google adds privacy noise. A Trends API alpha opened on July 24, 2025, with values that are not rebased on each call, allowing comparison across requests.

Search volume became a commercial metric with keyword advertising. Google's AdWords Keyword Tool and Traffic Estimator supplied volume and cost forecasts for most of the 2000s. On May 21, 2013, Google announced Keyword Planner, which "combines the benefits of the Keyword Tool and the Traffic Estimator into an integrated workflow," according to Search Engine Roundtable. By August 28, 2013, the old external Keyword Tool page displayed "Keyword Planner has replaced Keyword Tool."

The most disruptive changes came in 2016. Keyword Planner began combining volumes for close variants: "cat" and "cats" both showed 3,350,000, and "pay per click" and "ppc" both showed 135,000, while "seo service" (6,600) and "seo services" (27,100) remained separate. Ginny Marvin, writing for Search Engine Land, concluded that the volumes "should be seen as directional signals, not hard facts." Weeks later, Google confirmed that low-spending accounts would see ranges instead of numbers, and that the restrictions were "here to stay."

The tool was then rebuilt inside the new Google Ads interface in 2018. PPC Land's own records give two dates for the retirement of the old version: a May 2019 report that Google had deprecated it, quoting product manager Jane Kim on simplified navigation and improved forecasting, and a later explainer on keyword that places the deprecation in 2022. In July 2025, Keyword Planner added city, region, DMA and device breakdowns to its forecasts in select accounts.

Search volume drives budget forecasts, content calendars, keyword selection and market sizing. It feeds metrics further down the chain: impression share, estimated clicks and the traffic projections attached to SEO proposals. A mistaken volume can misallocate an entire quarter's spend.

The metric is also under pressure from changes in search itself. A Fractl study of 1,010,848 keywords using Semrush data, covered in PPC Land's report on AI's effect on search demand, found search volume had "declined 29 percent over the past year" as of April 2026, with FinTech down 37.7%. The same data showed declining and growing keywords roughly cancelling each other out, at about 10.3 billion monthly searches each, which Fractl described as redistribution rather than collapse. Google, for its part, said in 2025 that it sees "more than 5 trillion searches" a year.

The criticisms are long-standing. Grouping hides differences between variants that may convert very differently. Ranges make low-spend accounts guess. Third-party tools disagree with one another and with Google. Annual averages mask seasonality. And volume says nothing about intent, clicks or revenue.

Clicks are a growing gap. A keyword can keep its volume while sending fewer visits, as PPC Land's zero-click search explainer documents. Automated traffic is another open question. Investor Chris Camillo claimed in August 2025 that a single AI research request can spawn hundreds of Google queries, a claim PPC Land reported as unverified; Camillo disclosed a short position in Alphabet. If machine queries are counted, reported volume could rise without human demand rising.

Comparisons across platforms are also contested. Ahrefs estimated in February 2026 that ChatGPT handled about 12% of Google's search volume under its own classification, a figure PPC Land covered. OpenAI's Adam Fry later put ChatGPT's search-like queries at "roughly one-fifth" of Google's, as PPC Land reported. The two figures use different definitions of a search and cannot be reconciled directly.

Impressions. Search Console impressions count how often a site's link appeared on a results page a user viewed, for one verified property. They are not market demand, as PPC Land's Search Console explainer notes. Since June 2025, AI Mode data counts toward those totals.
Search interest. Google Trends' 0-100 index is relative popularity, not a count.
Search terms. The search terms report lists queries that actually triggered an advertiser's ads, not total searches for a keyword.
Keyword difficulty. A vendor score estimating how hard it is to rank, usually derived from backlinks, not demand.

Brave reported 2.7 billion queries for October 2026, up 56% from 1.73 billion a year earlier, a self-reported figure covered by PPC Land this month. Google's removal of the num=100 results parameter on September 14, 2025 forced SEO vendors to rebuild tracking, with SISTRIX founder Johannes Beus saying positions 11 to 100 were "no longer available," as PPC Land reported. That data also feeds many vendors' volume models. As of November 2026, Google has not changed how Keyword Planner defines average monthly searches.

Who: Search engines such as Google, Microsoft Bing and Brave generate the underlying data; Google's Keyword Planner and Microsoft's Ad Insight API publish it to advertisers; Semrush, Ahrefs, SISTRIX and others model it for SEO users; Amazon offers a rank-based equivalent.
What: Search volume is the estimated number of times a query is searched in a period, usually a 12-month monthly average, rounded and grouped with close variants.

When: Keyword-level volume has been available to advertisers since the 2000s; Keyword Planner launched in May 2013; ranges and variant grouping arrived in 2016; AI search has reshaped the figures since 2024.
Where: In ad platform planning tools, SEO databases and APIs, and in market sizing across search, marketplaces and, increasingly, AI assistants.

Why: It is the standard proxy for demand behind keyword selection, budget forecasts and content planning, even though every published figure is an estimate and says nothing directly about clicks or intent.
